problem: Learned visual topological navigation methods such as SPTM use image similarity or fixed-interval subsampling as a proxy for whether a node is reachable. Such systems do not scale with growing experience and break under nonholonomic constraints, actuation noise and unseen obstacles. They also give no probabilistic measure of plan uncertainty.
motivation: Topological, map-free navigation from RGB could remove the need for expensive metric SLAM hardware. The authors observe that whether a target image is reachable depends on the controller's own capability, not on image similarity or distance. For example, a far target in a straight hallway is easy to reach, while a near target behind an occluder is not. So the map, the planner and the follower should all be built around a learned estimate of what the controller can actually reach.
key_idea: Learn a Reachability Estimator that predicts the probability that a specific local controller (CNN waypoint predictor + RMP) reaches a target image, and use it as the single probabilistic metric for trajectory sparsification, graph construction and pruning, Dijkstra planning and robust path following.
insight: Explicitly modelling the controller's success probability lets the map sparsify adaptively. Anchors become dense in tight spaces and corners and sparse in open hallways. The resulting graph has less than 1/10 of the vertices and 1/100 of the edges of a dense graph, and grows sublinearly with the number of observations. Fixed-interval subsampling (SPTM) degrades earlier as sparsity rises, and the gap widens for weaker, short-context controllers. Two further ablations matter. First, predicting waypoints and letting an RMP controller handle dynamics and obstacles beats direct low-level control (Table I: 88% vs 46% at k=0). Second, temporal context frames around the target raise robustness (Table I: k=0 88% → k=2 91% → k=5 95%; cover rate >95% with context vs at most 90% without). Path probability computed as the product of RE edge probabilities tracks the empirical success rate (Fig. 9). With only 60% of the trajectories the planner is already close to its peak success rate, showing it can compose trajectories into new routes.
method: Two-stage local controller C = C_RMP(C_WP(o_current, o_target)): a CNN predicts a rough waypoint (x,y) in the robot frame, supervised with A* waypoints. A Riemannian Motion Policy low-level controller (laser-based in simulation) turns it into continuous controls with obstacle avoidance and vehicle dynamics.

Contextified target encoding: the target is a sequence of 2k+1 neighbour frames spaced ΔT=3 apart. Each [o_current, o_i, o_current−o_i] stack is convolved into a feature; the features are fused by a conv and FC layers. Auxiliary heads predict heading difference (cos, sin) and mutual image overlap (R_current→target, R_target→current) for proximity estimation.

Reachability Estimator RE: same architecture as C_WP but outputs P(reach | o_current, o_target, C). It is trained with binary cross-entropy on actual rollouts of C. Success means reaching the target within t_max = A* length / v_min; pairs are sampled 0.6 same-trajectory and 0.4 cross-trajectory.
Adaptive trajectory sparsification: the next anchor is chosen greedily as the farthest frame j such that RE(o_i, o_k) > p_sparsify for all intermediate frames k.

Compact probabilistic topological map: a directed graph with edge weight −log RE. It is built incrementally with edge pruning (RE < p_edge dropped) and vertex reuse (skip an anchor if an existing vertex bridges its neighbours with RE > p_reuse). The graph converges in static environments.

Planning and aliasing: Dijkstra on negative log-probability gives the most confident path and its success probability. Ambiguity is reduced by matching sequences of anchors and by re-planning when the robot stays in dead reckoning too long.

Trajectory follower state machine: Search picks the best anchor with RE > p_search. Follow advances the active anchor using RE > p_follow plus overlap-based last-visited localization. Dead reckoning tracks the last waypoint via odometry under transient disturbances.

setting.backbone: Custom CNN waypoint predictor (C_WP) + CNN reachability estimator (RE), trained from scratch; low-level Riemannian Motion Policy controller (laser RMP in simulation)
setting.training_data: 100k A*-planner trajectories (A* waypoints + laser RMP controller) in 12 Gibson environments; ~1.5M sampled image pairs with jittered start pose/orientation; RE labels come from rollouts of the controller
setting.observation: monocular RGB 64×64, 120° HFOV (goal given as an image); low-level RMP uses 1D laser scan in simulation; odometry for dead reckoning. A laser-input variant (64-point 240° 1D depth) is also shown for sparsification
setting.action_space: predicted local waypoints (x,y) executed by an RMP controller producing continuous controls for a nonholonomic car (forward acceleration, steering velocity), 10 Hz
setting.privileged: pre-collected experience trajectories used to build the topological map (90 trajectories between 10 locations per Gibson env; 7 manually driven trajectories on the real car); laser scans for the low-level RMP controller in simulation; no GT pose or global coordinates

numbers_note: Trajectory-following cover rate versus sparsity (500 trajectories, avg 15 m, 5 test envs) appears only in Fig. 7; the text says only 'higher than 95% cover rate' for k2/k5 vs 'at most 90%' for k0. Path-probability calibration (Fig. 9), pruned-graph generalization (Fig. 10) and map-size scalability (Fig. 13) are figures only. The real-robot map (206 vertices / 215 edges from 3,200 images, 7 trajectories) is reported qualitatively, with no success rate. This is a custom image-goal benchmark, not a standard Habitat split.
results: In 5 unseen Gibson environments, navigation between places with a goal image reaches 84.6–95.7% success over 1,000 trials each. The SPTM baseline, re-implemented with the same controller and follower, reaches 40.2–51.3%. The method also uses much sparser maps, e.g. house24 with 900 vertices / 1,348 edges vs 1,688 / 3,668. The two-stage waypoint+RMP controller reaches 88–95% local target-reaching success vs 46% for direct low-level control. The simulation-trained model transfers to a real RC car without finetuning, planning novel paths and avoiding unseen obstacles.
limitations: Fails when the robot deviates too far from all graph vertices; there is no exploration to recover or to build maps autonomously.
Perceptual aliasing in strongly symmetric scenes (lower SR in space8/house75) and cyclic anchor-following are only partially handled; long-term appearance change is left to future work.

Requires pre-collected experience trajectories; the evaluation is a custom benchmark in only 5 Gibson environments against one re-implemented baseline (SPTM), and the simulation controller relies on laser RMP.
